records.title: [C6] Version the orderings that naming depends on
records.body:
Part of #3010 · class C6: Identity from counters, proximity or shared namespaces → provenance naming (ADR-0043).
**Phase 2 — algorithmic change.**

## Occurrence
`kernel/topo/provenance.go:145` — `lessPoint / edgeRankPoint / nameGroup`

## Problem
The geometric rank that disambiguates siblings sharing a parent set is `lessPoint` - a raw (x,y,z) lexicographic order on float coordinates, applied to `edgeRankPoint` (the curve's mid-parameter point). Both are unversioned: changing either silently renumbers every ranked key in every saved document, with no migration. CLAUDE.md requires naming orderings to be versioned and migrated in place. Target: stamp an ordering version into the rank token and migrate on load.

## Rule violated
> Naming recursion is bounded: depth limit, cycle guard, source cap. Orderings used by naming are versioned and migrated in place.

([ground rules](https://github.com/Oblikovati/Oblikovati/blob/develop/CLAUDE.md#kernel--host-ground-rules-for-extension-and-refactoring))

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The occurrence at the location above no longer exists (folded, deleted, guarded, or annotated as the summary prescribes).
- [ ] The corpus/regression test that covered this path passes through the general implementation.
- [ ] Net delta of recognizers / tolerance constants / fallback sites / type assertions in the PR is ≤ 0.
- [ ] `archguard` and the full local suite are green; coverage >80%, duplication <3%.

_Enumerated by the 2026-08-28 kernel-shape audit (source list `occ_c6_c8.json`, subclass `f`)._

records.title: Add the Kronecker operator family to pyeki.linalg
records.body:
The Kronecker family is the operator work that the rest of the `pyeki.linalg`
roadmap builds on. It is a **capability step, not an unblocking one**:
`pyeki.gauss` and `pyeki.eki` both run on the operators already shipped, so
nothing is waiting on this. Sequenced accordingly — after `pyeki.localize`
(#14), which has a demonstrated correctness consequence.

## Prior art, and why it is not a rebase

A first implementation of `Kron` and `KronGeneral` exists in the **closed PR
#2** and is worth reading for the reshape algebra. Its branch (`dev/kron`, tip
`53e675b`) has been deleted as too stale to build on, so read the diff on the PR
rather than checking the branch out. It was written against the pre-contract
operator layer and could not be rebased:

- it implements `cholesky()`, which the contract rework **removed** from the
  layer in favour of `factor()` plus a primitive `whiten()`;
- it overrides `supports()` directly, where support is now defined by hook
  presence with derived-dependency resolution.

Treat that diff as a reference for the arithmetic and write the operators fresh
against the current contract.

## 1. `Kron(A, B)` — the square, PSD case

Represents $A \otimes B$. **Convention: the first factor's index is the slow
one**, so block $(i, j)$ of the result is $A_{ij}B$, matching `numpy.kron`.

Implement `matvec` by reshaping the trailing axis to `(n_A, n_B)`, applying `B`
then `A`, and flattening back. Nothing of side $n_A n_B$ is ever formed.
`solve`, `whiten`, `logdet`, `diag` and `factor` all apply to the two factors
separately, with capability resolution intersecting over them the way
`PSDBlockDiag` does.

:::{warning}
**A transposed orientation is silent.** It yields a valid PSD matrix with the
wrong meaning. Test `matvec` against `numpy.kron` directly, at leading batch
rank 0, 1 and 2. Do **not** rely on a `to_dense` comparison: `to_dense` is
built from `jnp.kron` of the children, a different code path, so it passes even
when `matvec` is wrong. This is recorded in `HANDOFF.md` under *Things not to
rediscover* precisely because the obvious guard test is vacuous.
:::

## 2. The rectangular variant — needed because factors need not be square

`factor(A ⊗ B) == factor(A) ⊗ factor(B)`, and those factors are not
necessarily square, so `factor()` must return a Kronecker product of
rectangular operands.

**The square implementation does not generalize.** It reshapes input and output
to the same shape; a rectangular Kronecker product needs the operand reshaped
to `(k_A, k_B)` and the result to `(n_A, n_B)`. Share one helper that takes the
operand and result core shapes as separate parameters.

## Interaction with #1

#1 as filed is stale — it describes a `cholesky()` method that no longer
exists — but its *second instantiation* is exactly this operator, and survives
the rework in a modified form. The Kronecker product of two lower-triangular
matrices is lower triangular and equals the Cholesky factor of the product
exactly (verified in #1: max upper-triangle magnitude 0.0, max error 8.9e-16
against a dense reference). So `Kron` has a genuine triangular square root that
the rectangular return type cannot advertise, and `whiten` must therefore be
implemented directly — applying each factor's `whiten` on its own axis of the
reshaped operand — rather than inherited. Settle #1 as part of this work.

## Then, in order

**`KronLMC`** — a sum $\sum_q A_q \otimes B_q$. For stationary kernels on a
regular lattice, circulant embedding gives a shared Fourier basis and the sum
becomes block diagonal with $n$ blocks of size $D \times D$
(`docs/design.md`, *Spectral (circulant) structure*).

:::{warning}
Circulant embedding gives exact `matvec` and exact **sampling** on the original
grid, but **not** `solve` or `logdet`: the grid covariance is a principal
submatrix of the circulant, and restriction does not commute with inversion. In
a one-dimensional check `matvec` was exact to $2\times10^{-16}$ and restricted
draws reproduced the covariance to Monte Carlo error, while the spectral
`solve` was 8% off and the log-determinant simply wrong. Either declare only
`matvec` and `factor`, or adopt the periodic covariance as the model — in which
case all four are exact by construction.
:::

**`KronPlusNugget`** — $C = K \otimes B + I_n \otimes C^l$ admits a
simultaneous diagonalization, giving `solve`, `logdet` and `factor` after one
$O(n^3 + D^3)$ factorization. Two preconditions from `docs/design.md`:

- The log-determinant needs the term $n \log\det C^l$, because the congruence
  $Q \otimes W$ is not orthogonal: $\log\det C = n\log\det C^l + \sum_{ij}
  \log(\lambda_i\mu_j + 1)$. **Omitting it is silently off by a factor.**
- It requires $C^l \succ 0$ on the whole block. A rank-deficient $B$ is fine;
  a *singular nugget* makes the pencil singular and no simultaneous
  diagonalization exists.

JAX has no generalized `eigh`, so compute it by whitening: Cholesky
$C^l = L_c L_c^\top$, standard `eigh` of $L_c^{-1} B L_c^{-\top}$, then
$W = L_c Z$.

**`LowRankPlus`** — last.

## Definition of done, per operator

- Factorization at construction time, in a `from_matrix`-style classmethod;
  never lazily cached, since a cache written inside a trace is discarded.
- Every instance through `pyeki.linalg.testing.check_operator`.
- A `matvec`-against-`numpy.kron` exactness test at batch rank 0, 1 and 2 — not
  a `to_dense` comparison.
- A targeted regression test for each silent-wrong-number hazard named above:
  the transposed orientation, and the missing $n\log\det C^l$ term.
- An entry in the operator catalogue with its cost, and a row in the contract's
  capability table.

records.title: [build-timings] Build Performance Report — 2026-08-27
records.body:
## Build Summary

- **Total build time**: 3m 47s (226.9s wall clock), clean `cargo build --workspace --timings`
- **Compilation units**: 372
- **Compiler**: rustc 1.98.0 (88d9e12ae 2026-08-18), cargo 1.98.0
- **Direct dependencies** (workspace depth-1): ~38 (41 lines incl. workspace crates)

## Top 5 Slowest Compilation Units

| Crate | Time | Mode | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `aws-lc-sys` v0.40.0 | 85.5s | run-custom-build | C/asm build script for `aws-lc-rs` (pulled in via `rustls`/`reqwest` TLS stack) |
| `libgit2-sys` v0.17.0 | 72.7s | run-custom-build | Vendored libgit2 C build (used by `git2`) |
| `syn` v2.0.117 | 26.7s | build | Foundational proc-macro dependency, blocks many derive crates |
| `rustls` v0.23.37 | 23.0s + 22.2s (2 builds) | build | Compiled twice — likely different feature sets across dep graph |
| `jsonschema` v0.46.4 | 22.2s | build | Large crate, pulls in `regex`, `regex-automata` |

Other notable slow units: `reqwest` (19.2s), `regex-automata` (18.0s, 17.2s — two builds), `clap_builder` (13.8s), `serde_derive` (13.0s), `toml_edit` (12.8s).

## Dependency Analysis

- `cargo tree --duplicates` found version conflicts for: `bitflags` (v1.3.2 vs v2.11.0), `regex-syntax`/`regex`/`regex-automata` chain reused with dev-only test deps (`cucumber`, `assert_cmd`), `semver` (two v1.0.27 resolutions via different paths — same version, not a real duplicate), `thiserror` (v1.0.69 via `gherkin`/dev-deps vs v2.0.18 used by workspace crates), `tower` (v0.4.13 via `tower-lsp` vs v0.5.3 via `reqwest`/`tower-http`).
- The `thiserror` v1/v2 split and `tower` v0.4/v0.5 split are the most actionable — both add extra compilation units and are only combined because `tower-lsp` (LSP support) still depends on old majors while `reqwest`/newer deps use current majors.
- `multiple_crate_versions` clippy::cargo lint is intentionally set to `allow` in `Cargo.toml` since these are transitive and not directly controllable.

## Cargo Lint Findings

- `cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` — **clean, zero warnings** in ~1m50s incremental check.
- `cargo fmt --check` not run in this pass (no changes made); dev profile already tuned well:
  - `[profile.dev]` uses `opt-level = 0`, `debug = 1` (line tables only), `split-debuginfo = "unpacked"` — all good for fast iterative builds.
  - `[profile.dev.package."*"]` compiles third-party deps at `opt-level = 1` (better runtime perf / caching) while workspace crates (`libaipm`, `aipm`) stay at `opt-level = 0` for fastest recompiles — this is a solid, already-implemented optimization.

## Recommendations

1. **High impact — TLS backend build cost**: `aws-lc-sys` (85.5s) is the single largest compilation unit, a C/assembly build script pulled in transitively through the TLS stack (`rustls` → `aws-lc-rs`). If `reqwest`'s `aws-lc-rs` feature isn't required (e.g., FIPS or specific algorithm needs), switching to `rustls` with the `ring` backend or to `native-tls` could cut ~85s off clean builds. Verify this doesn't regress security requirements before changing.
2. **High impact — libgit2 native build**: `libgit2-sys` (72.7s) compiles the vendored C library from scratch on every clean build. Consider whether `git2`'s vendored feature can be swapped for a system libgit2 in CI (already partially addressed via `apt-get install libgit2-dev` in `copilot-setup-steps.yml`, but the crate may still vendor by default) — set `LIBGIT2_SYS_USE_PKG_CONFIG=1` or the crate's `vendored = false` feature where a system lib is guaranteed, to skip this build entirely in environments where it's pre-installed.
3. **Medium impact — duplicate `rustls`/`regex-automata` builds**: Two separate builds of `rustls` (23.0s + 22.2s) and `regex-automata` (18.0s + 17.2s) suggest feature-set divergence across the dependency graph (likely dev-dependencies like `cucumber`/`assert_cmd` pulling different feature flags than the main binary). Auditing `Cargo.lock` for feature unification opportunities could avoid compiling these twice.
4. **Low impact — `tower`/`thiserror` major-version split**: `tower-lsp` v0.20.0 pins `tower` v0.4 and `thiserror` v1, while the rest of the workspace uses `tower` v0.5/`thiserror` v2 (via `reqwest`, `tower-http`). This is upstream-controlled; no action needed unless `tower-lsp` gets updated.
5. **Low impact — leverage existing caching**: Given `aws-lc-sys` and `libgit2-sys` are the two biggest single costs and both are C build scripts (not affected by incremental Rust compilation), ensure `Swatinem/rust-cache@v2` (already used in `copilot-setup-steps.yml`) has cache keys that reliably hit for these build-script outputs across CI runs, since these costs otherwise recur on every cold cache.

## Trend

No prior `build-timings`-labeled issue content was accessible for comparison in this run (access restricted to issues with "approved" integrity level). This report establishes a fresh baseline: **226.9s clean build, 372 units, aws-lc-sys and libgit2-sys as top bottlenecks.**

records.title: Spec: Source replaces containment (folders, entries, entities unified under one Source reference)
records.body:
> Spec produced by a grilling session (design interview). Every decision below was explicitly settled with the product owner. Companion docs: [ADR 0026 — Source Replaces Containment](docs/adr/0026-source-replaces-containment.md) (supersedes ADR 0005), glossary terms **Source** and **Source Path** in `CONTEXT.md`.

## Problem Statement

Today, "where does this item live" is expressed by three parallel mechanisms that can drift apart: a folder reference on every entry and entity, a `source_entry` reference on entities registered inside an ELN entry, and a soft display-ID reference in result properties tying results to their source entity. Entries and entities are forced to live in a Folder, so:

- The Library can only show Folders and Entries — never what an entry produced.
- Entities registered in an entry are placed in a folder and only loosely tied back to the entry.
- Results are tied to their source entity informally (a properties value), with no structural containment.
- The status cascade is hardcoded to one level (entry → its registered entities); results never follow.

Users cannot see or navigate the natural structure of their work: entry → registered entities → results.

## Solution

Replace all containment with a single required polymorphic **Source** reference on every Folder, Notebook Entry, and Entity. A Source may be a Project, Folder, Notebook Entry, or Entity. Projects are the only roots and carry no Source. "Lives at project root" means the Source *is* the Project.

- Entry's Source = Folder; entities registered in that entry get the entry as Source; results get their source entity as Source.
- A Folder's Library listing is exactly the items whose Source is that Folder. Rows with children expand into indented Source subtrees, recursively.
- Each sourced item carries a **Source Path** (ordered `{kind, id}` ancestor segments) maintained synchronously by the system — no recursive lookups for breadcrumbs or subtree checks.
- One generic "children of X" endpoint (optional recursion) replaces the Library contents endpoint.
- Status changes cascade down the entire Source subtree; deletion cascade-deletes the entire Source subtree.

## User Stories

1. As a researcher, I want an ELN entry created in a folder to have that folder as its Source, so that it appears in that folder in the Library.
2. As a researcher, I want an entry created at project root to have the Project as its Source, so that I don't need a folder for everything.
3. As a researcher, I want entities registered via a Registry Table to get the containing entry as their Source, so that the entry's subtree shows everything produced in it.
4. As a researcher, I want results registered via a Result Table to get the entity from the Entity Column as their Source, so that results live under their source entity.
5. As a researcher, I want the Entity Column to remain user-filled while the Result Table auto-computes Source from it, so that the table stays editable and containment stays consistent.
6. As a researcher, I want to expand an entry row in the Library and see its registered entities, so that I can browse what an experiment produced without leaving the Library.
7. As a researcher, I want to expand an entity row and see its results, recursively at any depth, so that I can follow long source chains.
8. As a researcher, I want expanded subtrees rendered with VS Code-style indent guides and slightly smaller child rows, so that depth is legible at a glance.
9. As a researcher, I want the expand chevron only on rows that actually have children, so that I am never misled about expandability.
10. As a researcher, I want entities whose Source is a folder or project to appear in the Library listing, so that API-created placements are visible even though no UI flow creates them.
11. As a researcher, I want my expand/collapse state kept while I browse but reset between sessions, so that the Library stays uncluttered by default.
12. As a researcher, I want marking an entry Finished to finish every entity under it and every result under those entities, so that one action closes the whole experiment.
13. As a researcher, I want to manually override a descendant's status, knowing the next upstream change overwrites it, so that I keep control without breaking the cascade model.
14. As a researcher, I want status cascades to never touch Folders or Projects, so that container-like nodes don't acquire lifecycle state.
15. As a researcher, I want moving an entry or entity (changing its Source) to update every descendant's Source Path immediately, so that breadcrumbs and access are never stale.
16. As a researcher, I want a move to never change any status, so that reorganizing never touches lifecycle.
17. As a researcher, I want deleting a folder, entry, or entity to delete its entire Source subtree, so that nothing is left dangling.
18. As a researcher, I want the entry and entity workspace breadcrumbs built from the Source Path, with entry and entity segments linking to their workspaces, so that I can jump up any source chain.
19. As an Entities Hub user, I want a Source column showing the direct source with its kind icon and name, so that I know where each entity comes from.
20. As an organization admin, I want access semantics unchanged (Project Grants plus Shared Folder subtrees, ownership never moves), so that this change neither widens nor narrows access.
21. As an API consumer, I want to set any entry's or entity's Source to any project, folder, entry, or entity within the same project, so that integrations are not limited to UI conventions.
22. As an API consumer, I want a single endpoint returning the children of any project, folder, entry, or entity — with optional recursion, so that I can fetch direct children or whole subtrees in one call.
23. As an API consumer, I want self-sourcing, source cycles, and cross-project sources rejected, so that the Source graph stays a forest rooted at Projects.
24. As a developer, I want Sour

records.title: Refactor orchestration for durable, truthful multi-bot workflows
records.body:
## Goal

Refactor and improve VelarixBot's current orchestration code, then evolve it toward durable, bounded, recoverable multi-bot development workflows.

This issue is the implementation umbrella. Work should ship as small, reviewable vertical slices rather than one large rewrite.

## Observed failure motivating P0

A lead bot delegated three read-only audits. All workers completed and persisted their summaries, but the parent response never reached the group room. The room remained on `thinking` while the roster reported the bot as ready and no session was active.

We need one authoritative, durable state machine from worker execution through result delivery and UI settlement.

## P0 — durable completion and truthful activity

- Persist a terminal completion payload before attempting parent/room delivery.
- Model explicit delivery states such as `result_stored`, `delivery_pending`, `delivered`, and `delivery_failed`.
- Make delivery claimable and retryable without re-executing the worker.
- Reconcile stale `thinking` UI from authoritative server state after reconnect/reload.
- Add typed failure reasons rather than parsing provider text.
- Track progress signals and distinguish slow work from stalled work.
- Preserve partial results when a worker is interrupted or stalls.
- Add behavior-level regression tests that reproduce the completed-worker/missing-room-response failure.

## P1 — orchestration

- Structured worker completion and blocker contracts.
- Durable task attempts, comments, dependencies, artifacts, and review transitions.
- Atomic task claims, leases, heartbeats, crashed-worker reclamation, retry limits, and circuit breakers.
- Per-task Git worktrees and role separation between orchestrator, worker, and reviewer.
- True bounded multi-bot rooms with deterministic mentions, serial rounds, pass semantics, hard caps, and needs-user escalation.

## P2 — specialization and scale

- Per-bot capability/tool policies and scoped expiring credentials.
- Planner/worker/reviewer model routing and per-task overrides.
- Prompt hierarchy with stable cached prefixes and repository context injection.
- Independent review workflow, bot routines, and optional multi-machine workers.
- Narrow plugin/skill boundaries rather than adding every capability to core.

## P0 acceptance criteria

- [ ] A worker may complete while room delivery is unavailable; its result remains durable.
- [ ] Retrying delivery cannot run the original work twice.
- [ ] Every run reaches a terminal or visibly recoverable state; no indefinite spinner.
- [ ] Reconnect/restart reconstructs the same run and delivery state from SQLite.
- [ ] Transient delivery failures retry within a bounded policy; auth/config/quota failures do not.
- [ ] Typed failure reasons reach the API and client.
- [ ] Targeted tests fail against the old behavior and pass with the implementation.
- [ ] Existing activity, lane, task, and reconnect tests remain green.
- [ ] Typecheck, inventory validators, lint/format gate, and relevant smoke tests pass on Node 24+.
- [ ] Security and QA reviews are recorded independently from implementation.

## Constraints

- Use strict TDD for behavior changes.
- Preserve existing activity/task history; use additive migrations for durable state.
- Do not rewrite or delete failed/rejected receipts to make recovery look successful.
- Keep work isolated in per-agent branches/worktrees.
- No unrelated UI or architecture cleanup in the P0 pull request.

records.title: P2: Add agent_* MCP tools backed by Pi coding-agent subagents
records.body:
## Outcome
Allow a trusted caller to create, observe, and cancel bounded coding subagents running through a Pi coding-agent integration inside the existing workspace execution boundary.

## Scope
- Evaluate the supported Pi SDK integration path versus its RPC/CLI mode; prefer a library interface when it preserves cancellation, streaming, and resource isolation.
- Define a small MCP surface such as agent_spawn, agent_status, agent_logs, agent_message, agent_cancel, and agent_list.
- Bind every agent to a principal, workspace, task lineage, TTL, output/token/cost budgets, allowed model/provider configuration, and explicit tool policy.
- Run Pi inside an executor or dedicated agent worker that has no control-plane credentials, Docker socket, or unrestricted network.
- Persist only bounded metadata, logs, artifacts, and redacted provenance; specify restart and unknown-outcome semantics.
- Add parent-child cancellation, concurrency admission, cleanup, and adversarial prompt/tool tests.

## Acceptance criteria
- Subagents cannot access another workspace, principal, or control-plane secret.
- Spawn/retry semantics cannot silently create duplicate side-effecting work without an idempotency key and status lookup.
- Parent close or TTL terminates child agents and descendants deterministically.
- The public tool list, schemas, annotations, and E2E behavior remain in parity.

## Dependencies
Build on #11 and align principal/provider credential policy with #13.

## References
Pi documents an SDK-oriented AgentSession path as well as RPC/CLI integration; select and pin the supported boundary during design:
https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/sdk.md

records.title: Alpha reliability: stress post-turn backlog, cumulative catch-up, contradiction repair, and retcon convergence
records.body:
Parent epic: #186

## Outcome
Long-running campaigns remain coherent when post-turn repeatedly fails/lags, newer gameplay continues, contradictions are introduced/detected, and repairs/retcons must converge multiple dependent state layers.

## Context
The memory system's trust claim depends on cumulative catch-up and evidence-based repair, not merely successful happy-path memory writes. Alpha should deliberately create backlog, identity conflicts, stale summaries/embeddings, clock inconsistencies, and visible contradictions.

## Scope
- Build stress scenarios that fail post-turn across multiple batches while committed gameplay continues within safe lag.
- Verify checkpoint remains at the last fully processed sequence and later runs cover the entire outstanding range.
- Inject entity identity conflicts, false player claims, NPC deception, stale derived summaries, hidden clock inconsistencies, current-scene contradictions, and delayed hidden consequences conflicting with newer canon.
- Exercise deterministic repairs, DM-adjudicated repairs, explicit retcons, directive consumption, and summary/embedding rebuild.
- Verify privacy/knowledge does not broaden during repair.
- Test safe-lag backpressure when accumulated context exceeds configured budget.

## Out of scope
- Evaluating storytelling quality unrelated to memory consistency.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Multiple failed post-turn batches later converge without skipped event ranges.
- [ ] Duplicate retries do not duplicate facts/entities/clock advancement.
- [ ] Delayed hidden consequences cannot overwrite newer visible canon.
- [ ] Repairs propagate to affected current state, graph/facts, summaries, embeddings, clocks, and projections as registered.
- [ ] Explicit retcon preserves superseded provenance while establishing one coherent current truth.
- [ ] Secret repairs remain visibility-safe and do not automatically grant character knowledge.
- [ ] Safe-lag threshold blocks new AI progression before required unprocessed context is omitted.

## Failure / recovery
- Test harness records checkpoint/range/repair state after each injected failure and verifies eventual convergence rather than only final success.

## Security / privacy
- Use synthetic secret/private scenarios and assert per-user projections throughout repair cycles.

## Observability
- Track backlog span/age, run attempts, repair incidents, retcons, convergence duration, derived rebuilds, backpressure duration, and unresolved incident count.

## Dependencies
- #216–#222 post-turn/repair.
- #209–#215 world/knowledge.
- #252 secret leak/repair controls.

## Verification
- Repeated randomized stress runs with injected post-turn failures/conflicts; compare final current state/provenance/checkpoint against expected authoritative history.

records.title: [auth-drizzle] DrizzleRoleRegistry ignores inherited role permissions
records.body:
## Priority
P1

## Problem
`DrizzleRoleRegistry.getRolePermissions` returns only a role's direct permissions and ignores `RoleDefinition.inherits`. This diverges from the auth-core reference `RoleRegistry`, which recursively unions inherited-role permissions and detects cycles with `visited`. An application that swaps the in-memory/reference registry for the Drizzle registry therefore silently loses inherited permissions for every user assigned a derived role. This is an authorization regression, not a storage-only difference: permission checks receive an incomplete effective permission set.

## Evidence
- `packages/auth-drizzle/src/libs/DrizzleRoleRegistry.ts:61-78`: definitions are registered with the full `RoleDefinition`, but `getRolePermissions` returns only `definition?.permissions ?? []`; it never reads `inherits`.
- `packages/auth-core/src/libs/rbac/Role.ts:15-38`: reference `RoleRegistry.getRolePermissions` recursively traverses `role.inherits`, unions permissions, and prevents cycles with `visited`.
- `packages/auth-drizzle/src/tests/DrizzleRoleRegistry.spec.ts`: no inherited-role scenario is covered.

## Reproduction
1. Register `editor` with permissions `['read', 'write']`.
2. Register `admin` with permissions `['manage']` and `inherits: ['editor']`.
3. Call `DrizzleRoleRegistry.getRolePermissions('admin')`.
4. Observed: `['manage']`. Expected, consistent with `RoleRegistry`: `['manage', 'read', 'write']`.

## Impact
Derived roles lose permissions when backed by Drizzle, denying legitimate operations and making authorization behavior depend on the registry implementation. A migration from the reference registry changes access decisions without any role-definition change.

## Proposed fix
Implement the same recursive inheritance traversal and cycle detection as auth-core's `RoleRegistry.getRolePermissions`, preserving direct permissions and deduplicating inherited permissions.

## Acceptance criteria
- Drizzle registry returns the transitive union of direct and inherited permissions.
- Cyclic inheritance terminates safely.
- Direct-only role behavior is unchanged.
- Drizzle and auth-core registries produce the same effective permissions for the same definitions.

## Validation
`pnpm --filter @croco/auth-drizzle test`
- Add direct, transitive, duplicate-permission, and cyclic-inheritance cases.

## Scope boundaries
Does not persist role definitions or alter role assignment queries; only aligns effective-permission resolution with the auth-core registry contract.

records.title: Evidence-gated extensions: durable task state, zero-token supervision, verification feature maps, and risk-triggered blast-radius proof
records.body:
## Objective

Evaluate and implement only the smallest extensions that can improve **cost per accepted task without reducing result quality**. The null hypothesis is **do nothing**. Every increment in this issue must independently defeat that null with measured evidence or a clearly necessary trust-boundary property.

This issue follows a comparison/adversarial review of:

- `dachent/model_proctor` current `runner/` architecture
- `kunchenguid/firstmate` event-driven / zero-token supervision and durable wake queue
- Cursor `pstack` verification-skill / feature-map approach
- Cursor `pstack` blast-radius workflow
- `dachent/skills/code-mapper-skill`
- `michael-denyer/pstack-claude` portability patterns

The goal is **not** to make model-proctor a richer multi-agent framework. Its purpose remains narrower: use the cheapest model that can reliably own a task, verify deterministically, escalate only when evidence requires it, and minimize total cost per accepted task relative to simply using the highest-end model for everything.

---

# Why this issue exists

The current runner already has strong properties that must not be weakened:

- deterministic task-start lane selection;
- cheap task-owning worker by default for bounded/spec-complete tasks;
- sealed verifier inputs outside the worker-writable tree;
- exact-tree acceptance receipts that stale on mutation;
- deterministic failure fingerprints / bounded switching;
- append-only metered task accounting;
- runner state outside the workspace;
- no worker self-acceptance.

The repository's own dogfooding also surfaced the largest measured cost failure: on the heaviest observed day, the persistent leader dominated spend (~96% of total) while delegated workers were cheap. That makes **leader-context residency** a legitimate optimization target. At the same time, prior work already demonstrated that adding routing/orchestration layers can increase cost. Therefore any new supervisor, queue, reviewer, mapper, or verification layer must be treated as suspect until it proves otherwise.

The proposed extensions fall into two distinct categories:

1. **Cost/control-plane extensions** — durable state + event-driven supervision, inspired by firstmate.
2. **Verification-completeness extensions** — project feature maps and risk-triggered semantic blast-radius proof, inspired by pstack but constrained by model-proctor's trust boundary.

They must not be conflated into one always-on orchestration stack.

---

# Adversarial review: conclusions

## A. Zero-token supervision is valuable only if there is something to supervise asynchronously

Firstmate's watcher is compelling because it waits in shell/OS code, persists actionable wakes before advancing detector state, and wakes a model only when intervention is actually required.

However, model-proctor's current `runner dispatch` is synchronous: the runner invokes the delegate subprocess and waits for completion. Simply adding a watcher around this path does **not** eliminate leader residency by itself; it risks introducing:

- a second state machine;
- duplicate liveness logic;
- race conditions between runner state and watcher state;
- extra persistence/reconciliation code;
- more failure modes on short tasks where waiting is already cheap.

**Conclusion:** do not add an always-on supervisor to the existing bounded lane. First make long-running work resumable/detachable behind an explicit feature gate, then test whether tokenless waiting improves total cost.

## B. Durable event history and current state should not become two competing sources of truth

Firstmate's durable wake queue solves a real recovery problem, but directly copying its fleet-oriented machinery would be excessive for model-proctor.

The clean adaptation is:

- an append-only task event journal as audit/replay evidence;
- one deterministic materialized projection used for current state;
- the projection must be rebuildable from the journal;
- LLM context is never authoritative state.

Avoid an independent queue, independent mutable status files, and current `state.json` all being separately authoritative.

## C. Verification feature maps can improve completeness but can also create dangerous false assurance

pstack's verification-skill approach correctly asks a deeper question than "did the supplied test pass?": what user-facing behaviors exist, and how are they actually exercised?

But a generated feature map can become stale. If model-proctor blindly treats it as exhaustive, it upgrades a documentation artifact into a false security boundary.

Therefore:

- workers must never generate/modify the acceptance standard for their own task;
- feature maps must be generated/maintained outside task execution and sealed/versioned;
- map staleness must be detectable where possible;
- absence/incompleteness of a map must degrade to the current verifier behavior, not block every task or pretend coverage exists;
- the feature map is a **coverage-expansion input**, not acceptance authority by itself.

## D. `code-mapper-skill` and pstack blast-radius are complements, but model-proctor should not absorb code-mapper into core

`code-mapper-skill` already provides deterministic structural evidence: Grimp import graphs, Jedi references, AST artifact/API/event/model/process extraction, contract parsers, lineage, and optional CodeQL value/taint flow. It explicitly does not execute the target program.

pstack blast-radius asks a different question: what hidden semantic assumption could make this small change break behavior elsewhere, and can that assumption be disproven/proved by actually running code?

The useful pipeline is:

`diff/change -> deterministic code map -> semantic risk hypotheses -> selected runtime proof -> normal model-proctor verifier/receipt`

But importing code-mapper's Python-specific dependency stack into `runner/` would violate model-proctor's current thin/stdlib-only architecture and burden repositories that do not need it.

**Conclusi

records.title: PHASE 03 — Organization Settings, Categories & Document Types
records.body:
# **\[PHASE 03\] — Organization Settings, Categories & Document Types**

**Branch:** `feat/document-taxonomy-settings`

## **📍 1. Executive Summary & Context**

-   **Context:** Before documents can be managed consistently, each
    organization needs basic settings and reusable taxonomy for
    categories and document types.
-   **Business Objective:** Let authorized users configure the
    organization and maintain the categories/document types used to
    standardize document registration.

## **🏗 2. Technical Guardrails & Constraints**

-   **Architecture & Patterns:** Categories and document types are
    tenant-owned configuration data. Keep them simple CRUD resources; do
    not introduce configurable workflow engines or custom-field systems.
-   **Security & Compliance:** All reads/writes must be tenant-scoped.
    Restrict management operations according to the MVP RBAC matrix.
-   **Observability & Telemetry:** Log configuration changes that
    materially affect document classification or expiration behavior.
-   **Performance & Scalability:** Index tenant-scoped names and
    active/status fields used by selectors; prevent avoidable duplicate
    taxonomy values inside the same organization.

## **🧠 3. Scope of Implementation**

-   **Backend / Core Engine:**
    -   Implement organization settings read/update.
    -   Implement Categories CRUD.
    -   Implement Document Types CRUD.
    -   Define validation and safe behavior when taxonomy items are
        already referenced by documents.
-   **Frontend / Client Experience:**
    -   Implement Settings \> Organization.
    -   Implement Categories management screen.
    -   Implement Document Types management screen.
    -   Provide create/edit forms, validation, empty states,
        confirmation dialogs, and usage-safe delete/archive feedback.
-   **Data / Infrastructure:**
    -   Create/finalize `organization_settings`, `categories`, and
        `document_types` tables.
    -   Add tenant-scoped uniqueness/indexes and soft-delete/archive
        behavior where defined.
    -   Keep expiration configuration compatible with the later
        expiration-engine phase.

## **⚠️ 4. Edge Cases & Risk Analysis**

-   **Potential Pitfalls:** Deleting taxonomy referenced by documents,
    duplicate names, tenant leakage in dropdowns, or changing settings
    that retroactively produce inconsistent UI.
-   **Fallback Strategy:** Prefer deactivate/archive over destructive
    deletion when referenced; validate all references server-side and
    preserve historical document readability.

## **📋 5. Execution Checklist**

### **⚙️ Backend / Services**

-   [ ] Organization settings API implemented.
-   [ ] Category CRUD implemented.
-   [ ] Document Type CRUD implemented.
-   [ ] Reference/in-use constraints handled.
-   [ ] Tenant/RBAC tests added.

### **💻 Frontend / Client**

-   [ ] Organization settings screen implemented.
-   [ ] Categories screen implemented.
-   [ ] Document Types screen implemented.
-   [ ] Selectors and forms use tenant-scoped active values.

## **🧪 6. Acceptance Criteria (BDD / Gherkin Format)**

-   **Scenario 1: Happy Path**
    -   `Given` an authorized organization administrator,
    -   `When` they create a category and document type,
    -   `Then` both become available to document forms only inside that
        organization.
-   **Scenario 2: Validation / Error Handling**
    -   `Given` a duplicate or invalid taxonomy value,
    -   `When` it is submitted,
    -   `Then` the API rejects it and the UI displays a
        field-appropriate error.
-   **Scenario 3: Permission / Security Gate**
    -   `Given` a user without configuration permission,
    -   `When` they attempt to mutate organization settings or taxonomy,
    -   `Then` access is denied with `403 Forbidden`.

## **📦 7. Deliverables & Artifacts**

-   **Documentation:** taxonomy/settings API contracts.
-   **Environment / Config:** no new mandatory external integrations.
-   **QA Handover:** CRUD, reference-integrity, and tenant-isolation
    tests.

## **🏁 8. Definition of Done (DoD)**

-   Implementation is compatible with the frozen Prazordoc MVP
    architecture.
-   Unit, integration, security, and relevant frontend tests are green.
-   Flyway migrations are deterministic and validated from a clean
    PostgreSQL database.
-   API contracts and environment/configuration changes are documented.
-   No cross-tenant data leakage is possible in the implemented scope.
-   No critical security vulnerabilities, unhandled exceptions, or
    blocking accessibility defects remain.
-   The phase acceptance scenarios are reproducible in the local Docker
    environment.
